Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.15 2.4 Groups generated by sets Recall that the notation ⟨g⟩ for some g ∈ G means the group generated by g. It is the smallest subgroup of G that contains g. (You might like to try to prove this!) In particular, ⟨g⟩ = {gn ∶ n ∈ Z}. We can extend this definition to include more generators. For example, if g1, g2 ∈ G we can define ⟨g1, g2⟩ to be all possible powers of multiples of g1 and g2, like this: ⟨g1, g2⟩ = {gn1 1 gk1 2 gn2 1 gk2 2 ⋯gnm 1 gkm 2 ∶ m ∈ N and ni, ki ∈ Z for all 1 ≤ i ≤ m} It is easy to see that this is a group. But why stop at only two elements?! Definition 2.4.1. Let G be a group and let S ⊆ G. Then the group generated by S is ⟨S⟩ = {an1 1 a n2 2 ⋯anm m ∶ m ∈ N and ni ∈ Z and ai ∈ S for all 1 ≤ i ≤ m}. It is the smallest subgroup of G that contains all the elements in S. In particular, ⟨S⟩ ≤ G. A group G is finitely generated if there exists a finite subset S ⊆ G for which G = ⟨S⟩. We now have a way of finding loads of subgroups of a group—just take any subset S of the group and look at the subgroup ⟨S⟩. (This might sometimes equal the whole group.) Example 2.4.2. The Klein four-group is a subgroup of S4. It is the smallest non-cyclic group. It is denoted by K4, and is defined to be: K4 = ⟨(1 2), (3 4)⟩ As you can see, it is generated by the two 2-cycles (1 2) and (3 4). Written out in full, we have: K4 = {e, (1 2), (3 4), (1 2)(3 4)}. For a fun exercise, try to draw a shape S whose symmetry group is K4.
